title: Japan approves foreign resident visa renewal fee increases of up to 967 percent, starts soon
description: Fee for permanent residency jumps 1,900 percent. At a cabinet meeting held on the morning of August 25, the Japanese government approved a measure significantly raising the mandatory fees foreign nationals must pay when renewing or extending their Japanese residency visas, including those seeking permanent residency in the country. Under the current pricing structure, foreign […]
content:
Fee for permanent residency jumps 1,900 percent.

At a cabinet meeting held on the morning of August 25, the Japanese government approved a measure significantly raising the mandatory fees foreign nationals must pay when renewing or extending their Japanese residency visas, including those seeking permanent residency in the country.

Under the current pricing structure, foreign residents of Japan pay a fee of 6,000 yen (US$38) when renewing their residency permit or changing its status, such as transitioning from a student visa to a working visa, or from a working visa to a spousal visa following marriage to a Japanese citizen. That flat rate will be ending, and in its place will be a series of much higher, swiftly increasing prices depending on the length of visa being applied for.

● 3 months or less: 10,000 yen (67 percent increase over current price)
● 3-6 months: 18,000 yen (200 percent increase)
● 6 months-1 year: 25,000 yen (317 percent increase)
● 1 year exactly: 33,000 yen (450 percent increase)
● 1-3 years: 48,000 yen (700 percent increase)
● 3-5 years: 64,000 yen (967 percent increase)
● More than 5 years: 75,000 yen (1,150 percent increase)

The increase is even larger for those applying for permanent residency in Japan, for which the fee will jump from its current 10,000 yen to 200,000 yen, a 1,900 percent increase.

▼ This fan formed by 10,000-yen bills still isn’t enough to pay the new permanent residency fee.

The higher fees are part of a continuing trend for the Japanese government. This past June, the decision was made to increase visa fees for travelers from countries requiring one to enter Japan by 400 percent, which was followed up by the July announcement that the departure tax travelers must pay when flying out of Japan will triple.

The increase in residency visa fees comes at a time of complex, arguably distorted perceptions by many Japanese people regarding the financial status of foreigners in Japan. The weak yen has resulted in a surge of foreign tourists visiting the country, many of whom are enthusiastically enjoying sightseeing, restaurant dining, and other luxuries that are becoming increasingly out of reach for Japan’s middle and lower-earning households as inflation surges and wages for many remain stagnant. The exchange rate is also making it easier than ever before for foreign nationals to leverage their home country savings into purchasing homes and real estate in Japan, either for personal use or to convert to Airbnb-style vacation rental properties, fueling anxieties that yen-wealthy foreigners will drive up prices for housing. Combined, these factors make it easy to perceive, or paint, foreigners as uniformly financially well-off and benefitting from being on the opposite side of the coin from Japanese locals in the current economic climate.

What often gets overlooked, or is conveniently ignored by politicians looking to curry favor with their voting (i.e. Japanese citizen) constituents, is that the economic conditions that are adversely affecting the average Japanese citizen are having the same effects on the vast majority of Japan’s preexisting foreign resident population. The foreign convenience store clerk, English teacher at a Japanese high school, or study abroad program participant who found an office job with a Japanese company and stayed in the country are all getting paid in yen, so they’re not at all living high on the hog these days. It’s hard to say whether executing such massive increases in residency visa fees at a time when so many are already dealing with tighter finances would be better described as ignorant or insensitive, but it’s definitely somewhere on that spectrum.

It’s not like the Japanese government is giving foreign residents much time to sort out how they’re going to manage these higher fees, either. Again, the new pricing structure was announced on August 25, and it will go into effect for renewal and permanent residency applications starting October 1.

At the August 25 meeting, the cabinet also said that measures will be taken to allow for reductions to the new fees for foreign residents judged to be facing financial hardships. They don’t appear to have gotten around to figuring out what the qualifying factors will be, how reductions can be requested, or how much the fees will be reduced, but surely those are top priorities for them…right?

title: Starbucks Japan adds new Customisation Bar to stores, with free ways to hack your food and drink orders
description: New bar helps to create up to 5.27 million possible combinations. Starbucks has been leaning into its customisations recently, offering suggestions on how to hack new limited-edition releases and exploring new ways for customers to personalise their drinks. Now the chain is taking things up a notch by introducing a new “My Customisation Bar” at […]
content:
New bar helps to create up to 5.27 million possible combinations.

Starbucks has been leaning into its customisations recently, offering suggestions on how to hack new limited-edition releases and exploring new ways for customers to personalise their drinks.

Now the chain is taking things up a notch by introducing a new “My Customisation Bar” at Starbucks stores nationwide, with five free items that customers can add to their drinks and food after making a purchase. According to the chain, when combined with the customisation options already available when ordering, the bar creates up to 5.27 million possible combinations.

The customisation bar is based on a concept seen at stores in the chain’s earlier days, when customers were able to freely add extras like milk, honey and cinnamon to their drinks. These bars were scaled back during the COVID-19 pandemic, but now Starbucks is reviving the concept on a larger scale, with two familiar favourites making a return alongside three new creations.

The two returning are: Honey, which is said to pair particularly well with the chain’s cappuccinos, and Cinnamon Powder, which goes well with a White Mocha, and any drink or food item topped with foam or whipped cream.

▼  The new offerings are Vanilla Sugar & Salt, Pepper Cardamom Maple Sauce and Ginger Sugar Chips.

Vanilla Sugar & Salt combines pink salt flavoured with vanilla and granulated sugar, creating a sweet-and-salty flavour with a vanilla aroma that goes well with a Caramel Macchiato. Pepper Cardamom Maple Sauce is a maple-flavoured sauce combined with black pepper and cardamom that’s said to pair well with both coffee and tea, and is particularly good in a Cafe Misto. Ginger Sugar Chips are small pieces of sugar combined with ginger, adding a subtle ginger flavour and a crunchy texture, and are recommended for a Coffee Frappuccino.

If the choices seem a little overwhelming, baristas are happy to share their favourite combinations, and Starbucks is sharing some top tips from three of its store employees.

▼ Global Barista Champion Nobuki Shimoide recommends combining a Caramel Macchiato with Vanilla Sugar & Salt.

The vanilla aroma and pink salt work well to bring out the caramel flavour while adding a sweet-and-savoury note reminiscent of salted caramel.

The chain’s “19th Coffee Ambassador”, Asumi Yamaguchi, recommends a Cappuccino topped with Cinnamon Powder and Pepper Cardamom Maple Sauce.

This combination is said to highlight the sweetness of the milk while leaving a lingering spiciness on the palate.

Ayaka Okamoto, from Starbucks’ Ueno Onshi Park Store, suggests giving a Vanilla Cream Frappuccino a more grown-up twist with Ginger Sugar Chips and Pepper Cardamom Maple Sauce.

The crunchy ginger sugar adds texture, while the maple sauce brings together the aromas of ginger, cardamom and black pepper.

Just reading those recommendations has us thirsty for a taste, and with the new options being free of charge, we can easily try them out on our next visit. Starbucks also says that special limited-edition seasonal releases may be added to the range in future, giving us even more ways to customise our orders without having to go through the potentially complicated process of explaining what we need to baristas behind the counter.

The My Customisation Bar will be introduced at Starbucks stores nationwide from 2 September.

title: Ministop brings bulked up Okinawan-style rice balls to mainland Japan for one week only
description: If you’re craving massive meals on a budget, portion-boosted convenience store foods are the way to go. On the days that you forget to bring your lunch with you, or you’re simply too busy to prepare one, Japanese convenience stores are like an oasis in a desert of hunger. Yet, while the portion sizes are […]
content:
If you’re craving massive meals on a budget, portion-boosted convenience store foods are the way to go.

On the days that you forget to bring your lunch with you, or you’re simply too busy to prepare one, Japanese convenience stores are like an oasis in a desert of hunger. Yet, while the portion sizes are reasonable for those with a moderate appetite, if you’re one of those with a penchant for big eating, the popular convenience store trend of boosted sizes is a welcome endeavor. From August 25 until August 31, the second phase of Ministop’s Zukkyun Increased Portion Fair will run, featuring five items that are guaranteed to leave you feeling stuffed.

Rushing over to our nearest Ministop, we checked out the latest lineup:
1. Tuna Salad, Ham, and Egg Salad Sandwiches for 321 yen (US$2.02), with an additional Egg Sandwich.

2. Okinawa-style Pork and Egg Rice Ball (with Barley) for 321 yen, with double fillings.

3. Super Spicy Mapo Tofu and Spicy Fried Rice for 645 yen, with 50 percent increased volume.

4. Spaghetti with Garlic, Chili Peppers and Sausages (also known as the Sausage Peperoncino) for 572 yen, with over 50 percent more pasta and an extra sausage.

5. Infinite Cream for 321 yen, with a more than 50 percent increase in the amount of fresh whipped cream.

Starting with the Sausage Peperoncino, which felt the heaviest upon picking up, the weight turned out to be an incredible 604 grams (or 1.3 pounds).

The taste didn’t give us any surprises, being a fairly regular convenience store peperoncino, but the addition of one extra sausage was pleasant. Rather than having an obscure ingredient boosted, the sense of getting a good deal was very forthright.

Next up was the Mapo Tofu and Fried Rice, also being quite hefty at 540 grams (1.19 pounds).

While it doesn’t quite reach the “super spicy” level it claims to be, it still has a fairly solid kick, being at a level that some people might not be able to tolerate. So, if you’re not comfortable with the heat, it’s best to steer clear of this one.

The selection of sandwiches may just have one extra egg sandwich added, but it is pleasing in its simplicity.

Unfortunately, the store we went to didn’t have the Infinite Cream available, so we were unable to include it in our testing, despite our tongues longing for the sweet, velvety texture of the whipped cream.

For our top recommendation out of the entire lineup, it has to be the Okinawa-style Pork and Egg, which is absolutely packed with fillings.

Taking inspiration from the classic Okinawan food of the Spam Rice Ball (“Spam Musubi“), this rice ball is definitely one you should try, without even having to leave the mainland. The secret to this dish is how they’ve focused on increasing the fillings rather than the total weight, delivering a very high level of satisfaction and capable of satisfying a light hunger with just a single piece.

So, if your stomach wants to join in the extra food fun, the Okinawa-style Pork and Egg is recommended for overall satisfaction, but the Sausage Peperoncino is best for its cost-mass ratio. The number of items in Ministop’s fair might not be large, but they make for an enjoyable lunchtime.

title: Dragon Ball Z theme park, financed by Saudi Arabia, to be built in France
description: “You know of my interest in mangas,” says French president. It’s unusual for a single franchise to get an entire theme park of its own. Disneyland, of course, is a place for not only the Disney animated catalog, but also the various live-action properties the company now holds the rights to, such as Star Wars […]
content:
“You know of my interest in mangas,” says French president.

It’s unusual for a single franchise to get an entire theme park of its own. Disneyland, of course, is a place for not only the Disney animated catalog, but also the various live-action properties the company now holds the rights to, such as Star Wars and the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Universal Studios’ attractions cover a wide variety of Hollywood movies, plus Nintendo’s Super Mario and a handful of other video game and anime IPs. Even Ghibli Park is a place for the celebration of the studio’s overall output, not one specific film.

But there’s a dedicated Dragon Ball Z theme park on the way, though it’ll be opening on the opposite side of the hemisphere from the anime/manga’s home country.

The office of French president Emmanuel Macron has announced that a Dragon Ball Z theme park will be built in the suburbs of Paris. The facility will be one of three new theme parks to be developed in Cergy-Pontoise, roughly 45 minutes northwest of downtown Paris, which will ostensibly sit on the site of the former Mirapolis, an amusement park which closed in 1991.

This news might have jogged your memory that there’s also a Dragon Ball Z theme park in development in Saudi Arabia, and the French park will also be built with Saudi money. The three-park project, with a total budget of 6 billion Euros, (roughly US$7 billion), is being spearheaded by Qiddiya Investment Company, a Saudi government fund with crown prince and prime minister Mohammed bin Salman as its chairman. Talks for the French Dragon Ball Z park began a year and a half ago, when Macron and bin Salman found out they had a shared love for Dragon Ball Z, and the announcement of the French park was timed to coincide with bin Salman’s latest visit to Paris.

Posting to his official Twitter account, Macron said “You know of my interest in mangas. You are also aware of my determination to attract investments in France that will create employment and make the most ambitious projects possible,” while claiming that the parks will create 22,000 new jobs (for comparison, Oriental Land, the company that manages Tokyo Disneyland, Disney Sea, and its associated hotels, currently employs around 27,000 people). Macron expressed his gratitude with “Thank you to Qiddiya and to Saudi Arabia for your confidence in our country, our talents, and our future.”

As for when that Dragon Ball Z-ified future is coming, there’s currently no timetable for the Franch park’s opening, but given the size of the project, it’s probably going to be at least a few years until it’s ready to start receiving guests, which should give Macron more time to practice his Kamehameha pose.

Source: Jiji, Asahi Shimbun, Reuters, Oriental Land Company, Twitter/@EmmanuelMacron

title: Japan tripled its departure tax to fund tourism but is using the money on cherry blossoms and bears
description: Questions are being raised over whether money from foreign tourists is being used as intended. On 1 July, Japan increased its departure tax for everyone flying out of the country, raising it from 1,000 yen (US$6.28) to 3,000 yen per departure, with the cost included in the price of the airfare. While the threefold increase […]
content:
Questions are being raised over whether money from foreign tourists is being used as intended.

On 1 July, Japan increased its departure tax for everyone flying out of the country, raising it from 1,000 yen (US$6.28) to 3,000 yen per departure, with the cost included in the price of the airfare. While the threefold increase applies to both foreign tourists and Japanese citizens, the government acknowledged that most of the additional revenue would be collected from overseas visitors, estimating they would contribute around 646 billion yen (US$4.05 billion) this year, compared to roughly 164 billion yen from Japanese citizens.

To soften the blow, the government told the public that the extra revenue would go back into travel-related initiatives, like lowering passport fees for Japanese citizens, and funding programs to combat overtourism, including the promotion of lesser-known parts of Japan. However, it was revealed this week that the 2026 fiscal budget, which was approved in April before the higher departure tax came into effect, also allocated departure tax revenue to cover the costs of bear control and pest prevention for cherry blossom trees – measures that are largely aimed at protecting the lives and environment of people living in Japan rather than improving the experience of foreign visitors.

According to Japanese media reports, the government allocated 6.2 billion yen for bear-related countermeasures in the 2026 fiscal year, with 6 billion yen of that amount coming from departure tax revenue. A newly created 600 million-yen budget for pest control of sakura trees is reportedly being funded entirely by the departure tax.

The Environment Ministry has justified the spending, saying that foreign visitors could benefit from countermeasures against bears, and many people from abroad come to Japan specifically to see the cherry blossoms.

▼ Foreign tourists aren’t the only people who enjoy the blossoms, though, as locals flock to see them too.

Bear encounters have become an increasingly serious issue in Japan, with both local residents and foreign tourists sustaining injuries from the animals, including at tourist spots. However, after news of the allocations came to light this week, questions have been raised over whether the heavy funding of bear and sakura pest control aligns with the original intention of the increased tax, which was introduced to fund tourism-related initiatives.

It’s also important to note that bear control and cherry blossom tree pest prevention measures had traditionally been funded from the government’s general budget, which draws on taxes such as income and corporate tax without being restricted to a particular use. Those defending the new funding argue that money from the general budget can now be used to cover other costs, but it’s unclear where the resulting funds will be redirected.

In light of these revelations, and amid growing concerns from the public, Japan’s Minister of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, Yasushi Kaneko, announced on 25 August that the government would consider reviewing how the money is allocated. He said the government would examine the spending carefully and work to ensure the money is directed towards projects with greater effectiveness and without raising concerns.

With tourism-related initiatives covering such a broad spectrum of issues that affect everyday life in Japan, it’s quite possible for the government to justify any use of funds if it has the slightest connection to tourism. As the government aims to increase the number of annual foreign visitors from over 40 million in 2025 to 60 million by 2030, the revenue collected from the departure tax is set to rise with it, making responsible use of funds even more vital to ensuring that the problems of overtourism don’t get lost amid concerns over sakura pests and bears.

title: Police in Japan looking for who’s responsible for dumping 80 loaves of bread on side of road [Video]
description: Weird crime could lead to seriously dangerous results. Tottori Prefecture’s Daisen-Oki National Park is one of the most beautiful places in western Japan, offering visitors amazing views of mountains and forests. Bizarrely, though, this month the scenery has repeatedly featured huge amounts of dumped bread. On August 14, National Parks Foundation workers discovered 30 loaves […]
content:
Weird crime could lead to seriously dangerous results.

Tottori Prefecture’s Daisen-Oki National Park is one of the most beautiful places in western Japan, offering visitors amazing views of mountains and forests. Bizarrely, though, this month the scenery has repeatedly featured huge amounts of dumped bread.

On August 14, National Parks Foundation workers discovered 30 loaves of bread that had been dumped along a 150-meter (492-foot) stretch of road that runs through the park. That might sound like the result of improperly secured cargo falling off a delivery truck, but the loaves were unwrapped, suggesting that they weren’t on their way to supermarkets or other retailers.

▼ As is the cultural norm in Japan, the collected evidence of suspected wrongdoing was arranged and photographed with care after being collected.

What happened next makes it even more unlikely that this was an accident, as loaves of bread were found dumped elsewhere along the road the next day, and the day after that, and then again on August 20. On those four days, maintenance workers picked up 80 loaves of bread from the side of the road, with a total weight of roughly 39 kilograms (86 pounds).

The repeated nature and large quantities might have one imagining that there’s a local bakery that’s tossing out the loaves that get screwed up during baking and aren’t fit for sale, but the abandoned loaves don’t appear to be malformed or otherwise obvious production failures. The discovery of 1.3 kilograms of dumped chicken livers and gizzards along the road on August 19 also suggests that this isn’t just a simple case of a bakery not wanting to pay for waste removal and deciding to litter the forest with bread instead.

Things get stranger still, as people on Tottori’s Hakuto Coastline, about an hour away from Daisen-Oki National Park by car, have also been finding loaves of bread dumped on the shore and in parking lots this month.

Now, if this were all taking place in a fairy tale world, where little children need to leave trails of bread to help them find their way home from an enchanted forest, there wouldn’t be cause for concern. In our real world, though, there are multiple problems that can come about from leaving large quantities of food waste in roadside and seaside areas. After enough time passes, the food will start to decay, becoming a smelly eyesore that’s also a health and sanitation issue.

Even before that happens, the food also has the potential to draw wild animals closer to human spaces, which can be dangerous for both people and the animals themselves. The Hakuto Coastline is a popular tourist destination, and anything that lures animals closer to roadways increases the possibility of accidents, either from them being struck by passing cars or motorists swerving crashing after swerving to avoid the wildlife. There have also been recent bear sightings near where the bread was dumped in Daisen-Oki National Park. With bear attacks having become increasingly common in Japan recently, the park’s administration, understandably, doesn’t want anyone dumping something that could attract the omnivores closer to roadways, and in response police have been stepping up patrols in the areas where bread has been found in an attempt to find who’s responsible, or at least dissuade them from continuing this bizarre behavior.

title: Pikachu and other Pokémon evolve into hydration types with Thermos drinkware collaboration [Pics]
description: A very cute, super effective way to keep your drinks as cold/hot as you want them. Every Pokémon species has a “type” that reflects its powers and abilities. As an Electric-type, for example, Pikachu can use attacks like Thunderbolt and Electro Ball. Fire-type Charizard’s repertoire, meanwhile, consists of moves such as Inferno and Heat Wave. […]
content:
A very cute, super effective way to keep your drinks as cold/hot as you want them.

Every Pokémon species has a “type” that reflects its powers and abilities. As an Electric-type, for example, Pikachu can use attacks like Thunderbolt and Electro Ball. Fire-type Charizard’s repertoire, meanwhile, consists of moves such as Inferno and Heat Wave.

But as of this month, several species of Pocket Monsters could also be called hydration types, thanks to a collaboration between the Pokémon franchise and Thermos.

Starting things off is a quartet of 600-mililiter (20.3-ounce) vacuum-insulated drink bottles, with the lovable and relatively small Pikachu, Eevee, Ditto, and Mew decorating their sides.

For especially thirsty fans, there are also larger 800-mililiter bottles. Two of the designs, with Charmander and Snorlax, feature jumbo-sized Pokémon in a thematic dovetailing with the larger bottle capacities, while Gengar and Mimikyu are here simply because they look cool.

All of the above will keep liquids cool at 8 degrees Celsius (46.4 degrees Fahrenheit) or warm at roughly 71 degrees Celsius for six hours. You don’t get quite as much six-hour temperature retention (10 degrees for cold liquids and 69 degrees for hot ones) with the following 500-mililiter three drink bottles, but in exchange you get flip tops, carrying straps, and multiple Pokémon per container.

▼ The designs here are Pikachu, the Eeveelutions, and one with a variety of species for Pokémon Trainers who’ve gotta love ‘em all.

All of these are great ways to keep your drinks at your desired temperature while on the go, but what about when you’re taking a coffee/cocoa/lemonade break at home or work? For those times, Thermos also has a line of insulated covered mugs, with Pikachu, Jigglypuff, Snorlax, and Ditto.

▼ Jigglypuff and Snorlax look like they’re already on break time.

And if you’ve got things other than drinks you want to keep insulated, like, say, some corn soup-flavored fried chicken or your boss’ frozen hat, Thermos can supply you with Pikachu, Psuduck, or Mimikyu insulated bags that measure 24 centimeters (9.4 inches) in length.

Prices for the bottles range from 4,400 yen (US$28) for the 600-mililiter models to 4,620 yen for the 800-mililiter and 4,950 yen for the 500-mililiter, while the mugs are 3,300 yen and the insulated bags 2,750 yen. The entire lineup is on sale now and can be ordered through the Thermos Japan online store here.

title: Turn octopus, spaghetti, and more of your favorite foods into crackers with Senbei Maker 2
description: You haven’t truly eaten a food until you’ve made it into a cracker. Who doesn’t love a good cracker? They’re dry, portable, can be customized with a vast range of toppings, or be used as toppings themselves. But the current range of commercially available crackers could be better. content:
You haven’t truly eaten a food until you’ve made it into a cracker.

Who doesn’t love a good cracker? They’re dry, portable, can be customized with a vast range of toppings, or be used as toppings themselves. But the current range of commercially available crackers could be better. It seems the cracker industry is largely hung up on cheese and salt for the most part.

But Japan’s premier random appliance maker Thanko has come out with a product that can unleash the full potential of crackers by allowing us to create flavors limited only by the human imagination. The machine is called Senbei Maker 2, wherein “senbei” is the Japanese word for cracker, although a senbei is typically thicker and harder than some conventional crackers like saltines.

The machine harnesses the patented technique of making any food of your choice into a cracker by heating it up and squeezing it really hard. The following video shows it in action, creating crackers out of French fries, melon pan, spaghetti, and whitebait.

With a little ingenuity, there’s no limit to what you can transform into a cracker. Note that while certain, highly mushable foods like french fries will naturally unify upon crackerification, some might need a little help. For example, in the video, a little batter is added to help the white bait stick together, and cheese can also make a sturdy and flavorful matrix.

▼ It’s easy as one, two, three.

Difficult-to-squish foods like walnuts or jawbreakers should also be avoided or pre-crushed into a finer crumb or powder so they don’t damage the machine. But other than that, you’re pretty much free to make crackers out of whatever you want. In fact, Thanko even suggests going ahead and tossing a whole octopus in there.

There’s no better feeling than being able to compress all your favorite dishes, whether it’s duck a l’orange or wasps, into edible discs that you can carry around in a file folder. Just don’t put a cracker in the cracker makers. That’s a paradox that might make reality collapse in on itself.

Senbei Maker 2 sells for around 5,500 yen (US$35) at various online retailers, including Thanko’s own website. It’s not clear what improvements were made on the original Senbei Maker for this model, making it kind of like the Evil Dead 2 of cracker makers, in which it’s hard to tell whether this is a true sequel or a reboot.

And also like Evil Dead 2, it doesn’t really matter, because its just a whole lot of gooey fun, so what are you waiting for? Pick one up and get crackering.

title: Data suggests increased bear sightings have led to a decrease in mountain climbers across Japan
description: In one region, the number of climbers has even decreased by an unbearable 34 percent since 2024. As bears have been increasingly encroaching on human spaces around Japan in recent years, the government has ramped up safety and awareness efforts and some entities have been going to extreme lengths to keep them away. The constant […]
content:
In one region, the number of climbers has even decreased by an unbearable 34 percent since 2024.

As bears have been increasingly encroaching on human spaces around Japan in recent years, the government has ramped up safety and awareness efforts and some entities have been going to extreme lengths to keep them away. The constant buzz of bear encounters on the news is why 熊 (“bear”) was even chosen as Japan’s 2025 Kanji of the Year. It seems that people themselves are also wanting to be cautious by staying away from mountainous areas, as data collected by behavioral big data platform Beacon Bank may suggest.

Beacon Bank tracked and compared trends in human movement patterns on Japan’s 100 Famous Mountains, a widely cited list compiled by a Japanese mountaineer in 1964, during the timeframe between April through June of 2024, 2025, and 2026 on national, regional, and individual mountain levels. The spring season was selected for comparison because bears are highly active then after awakening from hibernation to eat the plentiful mountain plants. To draw its conclusions, Beacon Bank analyzed the number of climbers who went within a 500-meter (547-yard) radius of a mountain’s summit using smartphone GPS location data.

▼ Bear warning sign on Mt. Bandai in Fukushima Prefecture

First, on the national level, the percentage of mountain climbers has decreased by 18 percent since 2024 (finalized data from spring 2026 is still forthcoming but preliminary figures suggest no net change since the previous spring).

On a regional level, the percentage of climbers has decreased most drastically in the past two years by 34 percent in the northeastern Tohoku region, where bear sightings have sharply spiked since 2023 when Japan’s Ministry of the Environment noted 20,513 sightings. In 2025, a bad harvest of acorns and other nuts that bears eat in Tohoku caused them to venture into more urban areas in the fall, resulting in a staggering 50,801 sightings. This year’s preliminary data as of August 6 indicates 6,260 sightings this past June, the highest level for the month since 2022.

In fact, Tohoku has consistently had the highest number of sightings across Japan since 2022, with 70 percent of them concentrated in the region during the surge in numbers last year. While we can’t confirm that the drop in climbers can be attributed to the rise in sightings, one might infer that locals have been playing it safe rather than sorry by choosing to engage in other activities than climbing.

Finally, on an individual mountain level, Beacon Bank published its findings of human movement patterns on 23 mountains with the most reliable data. As can be seen, out of all of these, Mt. Hachimantai in Tohoku’s Iwate Prefecture experienced the biggest percentage drop in climbers by 46 percent in the past two years. On the opposite end of the spectrum, Mt. Kaimon in Kyushu’s Kagoshima Prefecture actually experienced an 18-percent uptick in climbers over the same period.

▼ Much of the Tohoku region conjures up images of mountains and rice fields, such as in this view of Mt. Iwaki in Aomori Prefecture.

We should stress once again that the above data does not definitively prove that increased bear sightings have resulted in a decrease of mountain climbers across Japan as there could be other factors at play, but Beacon Bank calls the data “geographically consistent.” In any case, make sure to take all necessary precautions if you do plan on going mountain climbing in Japan in the near future by packing your bear spray and bells and downloading the bear sightings app before you hit the slopes.

title: Nephew of Studio Ghibli director Hayao Miyazaki serves up Totoro Shaved Ice in Tokyo
description: Find out if these limited-edition sweets uphold the family reputation for quality and creativity. If you’re a Studio Ghibli fan in Japan, one place you should definitely put on your list of places to visit is Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory. Currently owned and run by the nephew of Ghibli director Hayao Miyazaki, Shirohige’s has two […]
content:
Find out if these limited-edition sweets uphold the family reputation for quality and creativity.

If you’re a Studio Ghibli fan in Japan, one place you should definitely put on your list of places to visit is Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory. Currently owned and run by the nephew of Ghibli director Hayao Miyazaki, Shirohige’s has two stores in Tokyo – one in Kichijoji and one in Daita near Shimokitazawa – but the main Daita location is where fans are flocking to right now, because it’s the only place in Japan where you can get Totoro Shaved Ice.

▼ Only available for a very limited time, there are three varieties to choose from: Strawberry, Peach, and Matcha, priced at 2,000 yen (US$12.58) each.

We headed to the store to try the new desserts, and when we arrived at about 10:00 a.m., roughly half an hour before opening, there were already around 30 people in line ahead of us. It was a hot day, but staff showed a great deal of care for everyone outside, providing customers with cups of cold water and tea. Hayao Miyazaki’s younger brother, who ran the shop with his wife for many years before recently handing over the reins to son Yosuke, was also present, kindly handing out mosquito repellent to everyone in line, so the wait to enter the store didn’t seem too long at all.

▼ We placed our order inside, above the store’s signature Totoro cream puffs…

▼ …and were given two cards for our order – one peach and one matcha.

Artistic talent clearly runs in the Miyazaki family, as the menu and cards were beautifully illustrated. Creative touches can be seen throughout the store, and even outside, where the banner marked with the kanji for “ice”, commonly hung outside stores that sell shaved ice desserts in Japan, had been personally embellished.

This sweet message, penned and drawn by Miyazaki’s brother, shows the Catbus from My Neighbour Totoro being carried by Spirited Away’s Yu-Bird in fly form. Alongside it is the traditional summer greeting “暑中お見舞い申し上げます” (“shochu omimai moshiagemasu”), which expresses well wishes for the hottest time of year.

After admiring all the little details, it didn’t take long for staff to call out our order numbers and hand over our delectable-looking Totoros, which looked even cuter in real-life than they did in the pictures.

Starting with the peach version, which also happens to be the staff favourite, we were immediately impressed by the freshness of the white peaches and the beautiful hue of the syrup, which is made by simmering nectarines and plums.

Each shaved ice dessert comes with a beautiful white Small Totoro on the side, which is designed to sit between the larger Totoro’s ears, on a mint leaf.

▼ The Small Totoro is made using the same traditional nerikiri technique used to create moulded wagashi sweets.

It almost seemed a shame to interfere with such a work of art, but things were beginning to melt fast under the sunlight.

With the larger Totoro’s ears starting to disappear, the big eyes of the Small Totoro seemed to widen, as if imploring us to hurry up and eat it.

▼ Grabbing the spoon, we took a chunk out of Totoro’s stomach.

The ice was firm yet crumbly, creating just the right amount of texture to keep the structure sturdy and upright, giving us enough time to enjoy the accompanying ingredients.

▼ The peach was delicious – perfectly ripe with a fruity, refreshing sweetness.

The ice cream had a very pronounced taste of vanilla, as if it had been homemade, adding a lovely touch of richness to the sweetness of the peach.

▼ The bite-sized kanten pieces glistened in the dappled sunlight.

Kanten is a traditional type of agar, made from red seaweed, which is commonly used to make firm jellies and desserts in Japan.

▼ These were firm and smooth, with just the right amount of bite to help carry the flavour of the syrup.

The syrup really is the star of the show here, imparting a sweet-yet-tart fruity accent to the entire dessert. You could tell it had been carefully prepared, with the slow simmering process creating the perfect balance between flavours, and with just the right amount to take you through to the very last mouthful.

▼ Feeling refreshed from the fruity iced dessert, we were now keen to try the matcha variety.

This Totoro is surrounded by the same ingredients you’d see in anmitsu, a popular traditional Japanese dessert.

Setting it apart from other desserts, however, is the Totoro factor, with the large Totoro adding extra coolness to the already refreshing combination of ingredients.

▼ The mini Totoro wagashi adds a subtle sweetness and chewiness to the mix.

It’s the matcha that steals the show, though, with both the ice cream and syrup made with a generous amount of fragrant Uji matcha.

▼ The syrup pairs well with the anko bean paste, which retains a lot of the beans to give it a lovely coarse texture.

It’s also a good match for the kanten in the dessert, which consists of both plain and matcha varieties, adding greater depth and richness to match the bold flavours.

▼ Shiratama dumplings add another textural accent, and taste particularly good with a generous serving of matcha syrup.

Even when combined with the shaved ice, this remains a very rich dessert, filled with luscious, traditional flavours.

▼ Though the icy treat looked cute to start with…

▼ …it somehow remained cute right to the end, as the mini Totoro took a tumble and wound up looking as if it was swimming in matcha.

The Totoro in our peach dessert also dove into the syrup and ended up losing an eyeball, but still managed to look cute all the same.

Both desserts were absolutely delicious, and although we weren’t able to try the third flavour, strawberry, judging by the cries of delight from people who tried it nearby, it was just as good as these two.

Made with quality ingredients, the attention to detail in these desserts reflects the quality you’d expect from a place that bears the Miyazaki name.

The Totoro Shaved Ice is one of the cutest and best-tasting desserts you’ll find in Japan at the moment, but it won’t be around for long. Available on just six days, 21-23 and 28-30 August, the shaved ice is only being made in limited quantities so be sure to get there early to avoid missing out.

title: Nike x One Piece collection brings Devil Fruits to sneakers and streetwear in Japan
description: One Piece sets sail for global domination with a Nike collection inspired by the manga and anime’s superpowers. One Piece fans will soon be able to slip into some awesome powers from the world of manga and anime, thanks to a new collection from Nike inspired by Devil Fruits. The new Nike x One Piece […]
content:
One Piece sets sail for global domination with a Nike collection inspired by the manga and anime’s superpowers.

One Piece fans will soon be able to slip into some awesome powers from the world of manga and anime, thanks to a new collection from Nike inspired by Devil Fruits.

The new Nike x One Piece collection includes three special-edition Air Max Plus designs, along with jerseys, T-shirts, caps and a vest, with details that conjure up the supernatural powers received by consuming a Devil Fruit. While the collection will eventually be available globally, the first port of call is Japan, where customers will have the chance to get their hands on the collection ahead of other countries, at a special three-day pop-up in Tokyo beginning on 4 September.

The journey starts with Devil Fruit swirls on the kicks, which are priced at 27,500 yen (US$173.10) in Japan, or US$210 in the U.S. as the global standard pricing.

▼ Nike Air Max Plus SP “Gomu Gomu”

This purple-and-green pair takes its inspiration from Gomu Gomu no Mi, the Devil Fruit associated with Monkey D. Luffy, which gives him rubber-like abilities.

Whisper “Gomu Gomu no…” while wearing these and you’ll instantly feel like you can call upon rubbery superpowers to get you out of any sticky scenarios.

▼ Nike Air Max Plus SP “Ope Ope”

Berry-red and green hues conjure up the powers of Ope Ope no Mi, the Devil Fruit that takes you to a “Room” where you can manipulate objects and people at will.

While these sneakers won’t actually grant you eternal youth, they’ll make you look and feel young every time you wear them.

▼ Nike Air Max Plus SP “Mera Mera” 

The fiery orange, yellow and green colour scheme of the Mera Mera no Mi makes its presence felt on this bright pair of kicks, which will help to keep everyone out of your way whenever you step out in them.

The shoes are complemented by matching Air Max Plus jerseys and caps drawn from the Nike archive, which will be released alongside a range of exclusive apparel, so you can express your love for One Piece above the knee.

▼ Nike Solo Swoosh T-Shirt QS “Promise of Battle” (6,930 yen)

This eyecatching design, available in black and white colourways, features the pirate flag drawn by Monkey D. Luffy, with a large red Swoosh giving it a Nike twist.

▼ Nike Solo Swoosh T-Shirt QS “Gomu Gomu no Ono” (9,680 yen)

Luffy’s “Gomu Gomu no Ono” (“Gum-Gum Battle Axe”) gets the full manga treatment on this T-shirt, with a dramatic panel showing the stretchy pirate captain unleashing the powerful move across the back.

In addition to a couple of other yet-to-be-released T-shirt designs, there’s also an exclusive Nike Vest (45,100 yen).


The vest may be pretty hard to get in Japan, as it’s listed as a Tokyo pop-up exclusive and will be available at Dr. B’s Research Lab, a three-day-only pop-up store in Tokyo’s Harajuku district from 4 to 6 September. The pop-up will stock the collection as well as a special T-shirt exclusive to the event, but entry to the venue and purchases of eligible products will be limited to people who win the advance lottery (details at the bottom of this page), which is open for applications from 7:30 p.m. on 23 August until 11:59 p.m. on 26 August.

Fans in Japan who want to put their own spin on the collaboration can also head to the Nike By You customisation service at Nike Harajuku and Nike Umeda, where nine custom graphics will be available.

▼ Small graphics are 1,000 yen each, while large sizes are 1,200 yen.

The customisation experience will be available at Nike Harajuku from 4 to 11 September, with reservations accepted from 10 a.m.–9 p.m. on each day during this period, followed by Nike Umeda from 12 to 19 September, where reservations will be accepted from 11 a.m.–9 p.m. Reservations will be taken on a first-come, first-served basis until capacity is reached.

▼ Celebrate your own personal connection to One Piece by mixing and matching the graphics to create a one-of-a-kind T-shirt that’s unique to you.

As the first port of call for the collection, it’s a very good time to be a One Piece fan in Japan. Following the pop-up store event, the Mera Mera range will be sold at Nike Umeda in Osaka on 12 September, ahead of the collection’s global release through Nike’s SNKRS app on 25 September. Other countries around the world will also have their own pop-up events from 12 September onwards, so check the SNKRS app for more details.

title: Winnie the Pooh cosplays as Yuzuru Hanyu for new plushie collaboration
description: Apparently it’s not a bother at all for Pooh Bear to dress up like the Japanese skating star. Yuzuru Hanyu’s fondness for Winnie the Pooh is well known, and the Japanese figure skating legend’s fanbase has created a tradition of showering the ice with plushies of the character after his performances. content:
Apparently it’s not a bother at all for Pooh Bear to dress up like the Japanese skating star.

Yuzuru Hanyu’s fondness for Winnie the Pooh is well known, and the Japanese figure skating legend’s fanbase has created a tradition of showering the ice with plushies of the character after his performances. But is Pooh Bear himself one of Hanyu’s fans?

That might seem like an impossible question to answer, given that Winnie the Pooh, like most fictional animated characters, isn’t in the habit of giving interviews. But as they say, actions speak louder than words, and so it’s probably safe to say that Pooh likes Hanyu too, since he’s now cosplaying as the skater.

Publisher Kodansha is getting set to release To Pooh-san: Yuzuru Hanyu and Pooh-san Memory Book. The 40-page book contains a photo collection and exclusive interview with Hanyu, and to sweeten the deal, it comes bundled with a 20.5-centimeter (8.1-inch) tall Winnie the Pooh plushie. For this collaboration, Pooh is forgoing his customary red polo shirt and instead going with more fantastic fashions.

The plushie comes with two outfits, recreating the costumes worn by Hanyu at the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics, where he won the second of his gold medals. The ensemble Pooh is wearing in the above image is the same as the one Hanyu wore for his free-skate program to the musical piece titled “Seimei.”

And if you change Pooh into his alternate included set of clothes, he’ll match what Hanyu was wearing for his short program skate to Chopin’s “Ballade No. 1.”

Also part of the package are a 51.5 x 72.8-centimeter poster and reproduction of a handwritten note that Yuzuru penned to Pooh.

Kodansha is asking 22,000 yen (US$138) for To Pooh-san: Yuzuru Hanyu and Pooh-san Memory Book and its bundled merch, and all units are being produced to order. On the one hand, that means that pre-ordering is required, but it also means that actual fans are guaranteed to be able to purchase the set without having to go through a scalper.

▼ Yuzuru posing with Pooh dressing as Yuzuru…honestly, this does seem like a missed opportunity for the skater to have worn the bear’s shirt.

Pre-orders are open between now and October 20 through Amazon Japan and Rakuten (here and here), with Amazon listing shipping as slated for late May of 2027. And if you need even more Yuzuru Hanyu/Winnie the Pooh crossover merch, there’s the pair’s also recently revealed Shower of Heart collection.

title: Nagoya’s famous Shinkansen platform noodle shop has other, better branches nearby
description: Travelers love Sumiyoshi’s kishimen, but there’s a way to skip the long line and get a better deal on your meal. Nagoya an outstanding destination for traveling foodies, thanks to the city’s numerous tasty claims to fame, including tempura shrimp rice balls, a special kind of local miso, and a unique breakfast culture. Then there’s […]
content:
Travelers love Sumiyoshi’s kishimen, but there’s a way to skip the long line and get a better deal on your meal.

Nagoya an outstanding destination for traveling foodies, thanks to the city’s numerous tasty claims to fame, including tempura shrimp rice balls, a special kind of local miso, and a unique breakfast culture. Then there’s Nagoya’s representative type of noodles, kishimen, broad udon noodles with a soy sauce-based broth.

Kishimen is so strongly associated with Nagoya that you can even find great places to try it inside Nagoya Station. Travelers regularly form a long line outside Sumiyoshi, a stand-and-eat kishimen joint on the Shinkansen platform.

▼ The Shinkansen platform Sumiyoshi

However, while passing through Nagoya Station the other day we found out that Sumiyoshi also has kishimen stands on three non-Shinkansen platforms, and these are the better ones to go to, for two reasons. First, they’re less crowded, or at least they were when we stopped by on a weekday afternoon. At that time, the Shinkansen platform branch, as usual, had a line to get in, but we could walk right into the Sumiyoshi on the non-Shinkansen Line 5/6 platform Sumiyoshi with no waiting.

▼ The Line 5/6 platform Sumiyoshi

The other reason to visit one of the non-Shinkansen Sumiyoshi branches? The One-coin Kishimen, which is exclusive to the regular-line branches.

▼ ワンコインきしめん = One-coin Kishimen

The “one coin” here refers to the price of just 500 yen (US$3.15), which is also the largest-denomination yen coin. Suiyoshi already charges 450 yen for a bowl of just plain kishimen noodles, and most topping options beyond some simple seaweed will cost you 700 yen or more. The One-coin Kishimen, though, is a thoroughly satisfying bargain.

Along with the noodles, you get a nicely sized tempura shrimp, some aburaage (fried tofu), katsuobushi (bonito flakes) and sliced green onion.

This isn’t a mini portion of kishimen to make up for the toppings, either. It’s a full-sized serving of noodles, with barely any additional charge for all the extras that are in the bowl with them. And the low price isn’t the result of the non-Shinkansen Sumiyoshi branches using lower-quality ingredients or skimping on seasonings either. We asked the staff if there was any difference between how the regular and Shinkansen-line locations prepare their noodles, and were informed that they all make their kishimen the exact same way.

All it took was a single taste to confirm that the staff was telling the truth. This tasted every bit as good as the Sumiyoshi kishimen we’d eaten on the Shinkansen platform on a previous visit, just at a more budget-friendly price.

In addition to the Line 5/6 platform branch that we ate at, Sumiyoshi also has kishimen stands on the Line 1/2 and 3/4 platforms, and it’s a pretty safe bet that their noodles are equally delicious. And should you be looking for dessert afterwards, Krispy Kreme Japan has some special donuts in Nagoya that you can’t get anywhere else in the world.

title: Osaka Starbucks has one of the city’s coolest photo vantage points, but it’s going away soon
description: We head to Osaka to say goodbye to Ebitsuta, and get a new view at one of the city’s most famous landmarks. The physical media market definitely isn’t what it used to be. Back when he was a college student in Osaka, our Japanese-language reporter Seiji Nakazawa spent countless hours hanging out in the Ebisubashi […]
content:
We head to Osaka to say goodbye to Ebitsuta, and get a new view at one of the city’s most famous landmarks.

The physical media market definitely isn’t what it used to be. Back when he was a college student in Osaka, our Japanese-language reporter Seiji Nakazawa spent countless hours hanging out in the Ebisubashi branch of multimedia chain Tsutaya. Located in the Dotonbori entertainment district, Ebitsuta, as the cool kids called this Tsutaya, had just recently opened, and was stocked with so many CDs and movies to rent or buy that it felt like an enchanted forest of audio/video wonders. As an aspiring rock guitarist, Seiji regularly got blissfully lost looking through the gigantic music selection, and if he was meeting up with friends in the neighborhood, he’d often get there early and tell them to come find him at Ebitsuta.

Sadly, though, Ebitsuta’s days are numbered. With fewer and fewer people buying or renting physical media, Tsutaya has spent the last several years dramatically restructuring, and now the decision has been made to close the Ebisubashi branch, which opened all the way back in 2003. Thankfully, Ebitsuta will still be open for a few more months, which meant Seiji had time to go back recently and say goodbye, and also to find a great photo-snapping vantage point.

Since he moved to Tokyo not long after graduating, it’s actually been a very long time since Seiji stopped by this Tsutaya, and stepping inside, he found out that in many ways it’s already pivoted away from its former foci. The basement floor, for example, now houses the Osaka IP Shoten, Tsutaya’s sub-brand for anime character merch.

There is still a music vibe going on, though, thanks to how huge a presence virtual YouTubers, many of which have vocalist side hustles, now have in the otaku sphere. This Ebitsuta Osaka IP Shoten seems to be especially oriented towards female fans, with huge standees of male VTuber group Eden-gumi waiting at the entrance to greet shoppers when Seiji visited, and a comparatively smaller section for female performers.

Next, let’s skip ahead to the third floor, which is devoted to…

…cosmetics? At first, Seiji thought this might be a non-Tsutaya tenant who was renting out the third floor, but actually this is another example of the company’s evolving diversification, as it now has its own cosmetic retailing sub-brand, called @Cosme Store/Tsutaya.

Moving up to the four floor, Seiji found it pretty much entirely stocked with idol singer CDs, photo albums, magazines, and other related merchandise. It felt sort of like the flesh-and-blood counterpart to the basement level’s anime goods.

The fifth floor is an event hall, but with nothing on the schedule this day, it was closed to the public. So now let’s head back down to the first floor, where there’s a Starbucks.

In and of itself, that’s nothing to get all that excited about, since there are tons of Starbucks branches in Japan. Still, being in Dotonbori, this is a convenient enough location, and things really get good when you head up to the second floor, where there’s additional seating…

…and a fantastic view of Osaka’s world-famous mechanized crab sign!

The storefront of the main branch of crab specialty restaurant Kani Doraku is a must-see when visiting Osaka, and this might be one of the best places to see it from. When viewed from the street outside, you’re mainly only able to see the bottom half of the creature, and it’s not really visible from inside Kani Doraku itself. The Ebitsuta Starbucks’ second-floor windows, though, let you look at it straight on, allowing you to fully grasp its scale and how intricate its movements are.

▼ You can even see how its eyes move!

The last day for Ebisubashi Tsutaya will be January 11. It’s not clear what’ll happen after that, such as whether the building will be torn down for a replacement or whether new tenants will be moving in to a redistributed and renovated interior. That means that there’s no guarantee that you’ll be able to see this view of Osaka’s mecha crab landmark, so if you’re looking for a place to sip on one of those new Japanese grape Frappuccinos, we’d highly recommend this one.

title: We recommend not buying one pack of Japan’s new convenience store corn soup-flavor fried chicken
description: But that doesn’t mean we don’t love it. Japanese convenience store chain Lawson’s Karaage-kun is one of the absolute all-stars of the combini food world. These bite-sized pieces of karaage (Japanese-style fried chicken), which even come with a toothpick so you can eat them without getting your fingers dirty, are so deliciously satisfying that it’s […]
content:
But that doesn’t mean we don’t love it.

Japanese convenience store chain Lawson’s Karaage-kun is one of the absolute all-stars of the combini food world. These bite-sized pieces of karaage (Japanese-style fried chicken), which even come with a toothpick so you can eat them without getting your fingers dirty, are so deliciously satisfying that it’s hard for us to recall a time when we regretted buying a pack of them.

But while Karaage-kun is a reliable favorite, Lawson still likes to change things up by offering seasonal and limited-time flavors alongside the always-available regular-version Karaage-kun. That’s what brought us to Lawson on a recent afternoon to try their new corn soup-flavored fried chicken.

It might not be a standard-bearer for Japanese cuisine with such global fame as sushi or ramen, but corn soup definitely has a place in the country’s heart and stomach. Anyone who’s traveled in Japan during the fall or winter has probably spotted cans of heated corn soup for sale in vending machines, but you can find it year-round at restaurants that serve Western-style fare in Japan, including steak restaurant chain Asakuma, whose take on corn soup is so popular that it’s sold on its own too.

▼ Asakuma corn soup

You can find Asakuma branches in the Tokyo area, but the chain got its start in Nagoya, and so the Asakuma Corn Soup Karaage-kun is not only a limited-time flavor, but a region-specific one too, only available at Lawson locations in the Tokai and Hokuriku areas that sit between Japan’s eastern Kanto and central Kansai. We were willing to track it down, though, to see how it tastes.

▼ The box’s graphics sport the Asakuma (あさくま) logo.

Japanese-style corn soup, also sometimes called corn potage, is similar to corn chowder, but simpler, creamier, and slightly sweeter. It’s an accessible, widely loved flavor, but would it work well with fried chicken?

As soon as we opened the flap, the inviting aroma of corn soup wafter up out of the box. After spearing a piece of chicken, we popped it into our mouth, and just as our olfactory senses had been promised, this Karaage-kun delivered the gentle but unmistakable rich flavor of corn soup. There was nothing forceful or artificial-feeling about it, just a comforting, enticing flavor profile that smoothly accentuated the meaty notes of the chicken with those of sweet corn.

Just how happy were we with the Corn Soup Karaage-kun? So happy that we immediately bought another box, since we were absolutely certain knew we’d be craving more after we finished the first pack.

▼ Buying just one would be a mistake.

With the Corn Soup Karaage-kun priced at 298 yen (US$1.90), we also had room in our budget for another collaboration between Lawson and Asakuma, this one a 248-yen roll cake reimagining of the purin (custard pudding) Asakuma serves.

Nagoya is famous for the quality of its eggs, and their rich sweetness, with a touch of bitterness from the ribbon and drizzle of caramel sauce, make for an excellent dessert

Really, the only downside here is that these items aren’t available nationwide, so if you want to try them, you’ll need to head to a Lawson in Aichi, Shizuoka, Gifu, Toyama, Ishikawa, or Fukui Prefecture, or to participating stores in Mie or Fukui Prefecture. On the plus side, that means you’ll also be able to try the other Tokai/Hokuriku foods Lawson has in those regions right now, like the chicken cutlet sandwich produced in cooperation with Nagoya chicken wing specialty restaurant Furaibo.

And hey, if this gives you an excuse to combine travel and fried chicken, two of the finest things in life, then that sounds like a win-win to us.

title: Ohaw? Ruibe? Pocche? While traveling in Japan’s north, we try Ainu cuisine for the first time
description: Taste-testing the northern frontier of local foods in Japan. Just about every corner of Japan has some special food it’s famous for, and if you head up to the country’s northern tip, Hokkaido Prefecture, there are several. Travelers often arrive in Hokkaido licking their lips as they look forward to some of the country’s best […]
content:
Taste-testing the northern frontier of local foods in Japan.

Just about every corner of Japan has some special food it’s famous for, and if you head up to the country’s northern tip, Hokkaido Prefecture, there are several. Travelers often arrive in Hokkaido licking their lips as they look forward to some of the country’s best salmon roe, sea urchin, and crab, plus delicious miso ramen, soup curry, and all sorts of cheeses and dairy desserts.

But on our recent visit to Hokkaido, the most memorable things we ate were the ones we hadn’t ever heard of before this trip: ohaw, ruibe, and pocche.

If you’re an experienced eater of Japanese cuisine yet don’t recognize any of those, don’t fell like you’ve got to turn in your foodie card. All of those dishes come from the culture of the Ainu, the indigenous people who populated Hokkaido before the arrival of Japanese settlers and the region’s absorption into Japan. Though Hokkaido’s Ainu population is far smaller than it used to be, cultural centers like Akanko Ainu Kotan, near the shore of Lake Akanko, help to preserve Ainu cultural traditions and share them with visitors.

In addition to a theater with traditional dance performances and shops selling handicrafts, Akanko Ainu Kotan also has restaurants where you can try Ainu dishes, and with our visit coming right around launch time, we decided to check out the eatery Marukibune.

▼ 丸木舟 = Marukibune

After sitting down, we opened up the menu and took a look. While such standard dishes as soy sauce broth ramen and curry rice are available, we wanted a literal taste of Ainu culture, so that’s what we gravitated towards…

…and for our first step into this new-to-us food frontier, we selected the yuk kam ohaw.

Breaking that down linguistically, ohaw is a kind of stew made with fish or other animal stock and kelp. Kam ohaw means that there’s meat in the stew, and yuk indicates that the meat here is venison.

Our ohaw also contained root vegetables and wild garlic.

It looked very different from the sort of soups common to mainstream Japanese cooking, and we braced ourselves for something that could possibly be an acquired taste. That apprehension turned out to be unnecessary though, as we found it immediately delicious.

Despite the generous portion of venison, there was no gaminess at all to the flavor profile, which was instead fortifying yet simple and comforting. It was so good that we think we might find ourselves craving a bowl of ohaw once the winter chill sets in later this year.

Next up: parimomo ruibe.

Ruibe is the Ainu equivalent to sashimi, but with a few key differences. First, ruibe is prepared, and served, frozen. Second, while conventional sashimi consists pretty much entirely of saltwater seafood, ruibe is made with freshwater fish as well. In our case, parimomo is the Ainu word for the fish called Ezo ugui in Japanese (whose scientific name is Pseudaspius sachalinensis), a relative of the freshwater minnow.

Marukibune catches its Ezo ugui from Lake Kussharoko, which isn’t too far away from the restaurant, so it’s fresh and flavorful, with a sweetness that comes to a clean finish. The mouthfeel of the frozen fish slices, and the sensation of the texture changing as they thawed as we chewed, took a little getting used to, but made for an enjoyably stimulating change of pace from regular sashimi.

We also ordered a kotandon. This is a donburi (rice bowl) topped with strips of grilled pork, wild garlic, onion, and egg, flavored with a salty sweet marinade.

To be honest, we’re not sure exactly how traditional the kotandon is. In addition to being part of Akanko Ainu Kotan’s name, kotan is the Ainu word for a village or community. It seems like the kotandon might be a more modern fusion concession to visitors to Akanko Ainu Kotan who want something that’s a nod to Ainu culture but isn’t going to feel too challenging. None of that changes the fact, though, that this is a very tasty rice bowl, and one that just about anyone will probably enjoy.

And last, we ordered a pocche set.

That might look like a plate of cookies accompanying our cup of tea, but pocche are actually preserved potatoes. Hokkaido gets very cold in winter, and pocche are traditionally made by leaving potatoes outside until they freeze, then bringing them inside to thaw, and repeating the process enough times for fermentation to take place.

So rather than a dessert, pocche were actually a way to make sure the entire potato harvest could get eaten. They have a chewy texture but no sweetness beyond that which you’d find in a regular potato. We can’t really say they tasted particularly good, but they didn’t taste bad either, and they’re an interesting way to experience hands-on one way that the Ainu culture turned the harsh conditions of Hokkaido’s winter weather into a positive.

As for prices, our ohaw was 1,200 yen (US$7.50 yen), the ruibe 1,100 yen, the kotandon (which also came with a side of ruibe) 2,600 yen, and the pocche set 1,100 yen. Taking the portion sizes into account, those prices are a little on the high side, but it was money well spent for such a unique meal.

After eating, it’s also well worth your time to take a look at the rest of Akanko Ainu Kotan too.

We especially recommend the Ikor Theater, which hosts three different traditional storytelling dance performances.

Even without a reservation, we were able to catch the Ainu Ancient Ceremonial Dance program, which presents an inaw, a ceremonial tool mean to form a connection between performers and the kamuy (Ainu gods). The dances aren’t flashy, but seated in the theater, with the light of open-flame torches illuminating the dancers and singers, we were comfortably mesmerized for the 30 minutes the performance lasts.

As an added bonus, the nearby Lake Akanko is quite beautiful too, whether you’re admiring the scenery from the shore of from the deck of one of the boats offering cruises for day trippers.

So if you’re looking to broaden not only your cultural knowledge, but also your palate, while you’re in Hokkaido, stop on by Akanko Ainu Kotan and Marukibune.

title: Narita Airport Transit & Stay Program returns after six years with free tours and festival experiences
description: Immerse yourself in a lesser-known side of Japan, minutes away from the famous international airport.  Narita City in Tokyo’s neighbouring Chiba Prefecture tends to be overlooked as a travel destination, with a lot of overseas visitors bypassing it on their way in and out of the country through Narita Airport. The area around the airport […]
content:
Immerse yourself in a lesser-known side of Japan, minutes away from the famous international airport. 

Narita City in Tokyo’s neighbouring Chiba Prefecture tends to be overlooked as a travel destination, with a lot of overseas visitors bypassing it on their way in and out of the country through Narita Airport. The area around the airport really is worth exploring, though, as it retains a traditional charm with historic shrines and temples, a famous Edo-style traditional shopping street, and lots of special workshops and experiences for tourists.

To help visitors explore these charms, Narita Airport is bringing back its special free guided tours, which were introduced in 2015 but suspended due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Designed for transit passengers and foreign tourists staying around the airport, the “Narita Airport Transit & Stay Program” will officially restart on 1 October, after a six-year absence, with English-speaking volunteer guides providing free tours and an additional paid “Plus” series, for special experiences that reveal a deeper side of the area.

There are six free guided tours:

▼ Narita City (3-hour tour)

This tour takes you to Naritasan Shinshoji, a temple with 1,000 years of history, and the Omotesando shopping street, where you can pick up souvenirs and snacks at traditional stores.

▼ Naritasan Shinshoji is 25 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Katori City (5-hour tour)

Here you’ll find a riverside town with a beautiful traditional atmosphere, where you can take part in Sawara Hariko, a traditional paper-mache craft local to the area.

▼ Katori is 41 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Tako (4-hour tour)

Famous for its rice, this town boasts a beautiful green landscape and rural scenery, which you can easily explore by renting an electric-assist bicycle.

▼ Tako is 23 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Shibayama (4-hour tour)

Two of the highlights on this tour are a visit to the Museum of Aeronautical Sciences and a home-style buffet lunch, with a wide variety of local ingredients, on weekdays.

▼ Shibayama is 26 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Sakae (5-hour tour)

Slip into a yukata and step back in time at a beautiful open-air museum called Boso no Mura (“Boso Village”).

▼ Sakae is 27 minutes by train from Narita Airport

▼ Kozaki (6-hour tour)

Dubbed the “village of fermentation”, this part of Chiba prides itself on brewed and fermented products, with two sake breweries in the area, as well as miso stores and bakeries that use natural yeast made from sake lees (a byproduct of the sake-making process).

A visit to Kozaki Shrine is another highlight of the tour, and it’s said to be a good place for travelers to pray for safe journeys as it’s home to the guardian deity of aviation, transportation, and industry.

▼ Kozaki is roughly 31 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

Though the guided tours are free, participants need to cover their own expenses such as transportation, meals and admission fees. As for the paid Transit & Stay Program, there are currently nine to choose from, including a one-hour brewery tour and tasting for 1,000 yen (US$6.31)…

▼ … a knife-forging experience (4 hours, from 32,800 yen)…

…and entry to the World Boshuriken Tournament, where you can dress in a ninja costume and try out some ninja techniques for yourself (5.5 hours, 23,800 yen).

▼ What’s likely to really draw tourists, though, is the chance to participate in a local festival.

Pulling a festival float is usually only reserved for people who live in the neighbourhoods where the festival is being held, so this is a rare opportunity to immerse yourself in the culture and rub shoulders with the locals.

The first festival-focused tour to be offered is the Otaiyasai Festival on 5 September, which is being treated as a pre-official launch event. Taking around five hours and priced from 15,800 yen, this tour takes place at the Sogo Reido temple, which is half an hour by train from the airport.

Those pressed for time can enjoy a shorter two-hour float-pulling experience at the Narita Gion Festival on Omotesando Street from 8-11 July 2027…

… while those wanting maximum festival immersion can stay overnight during the Narita Gion Festival, with the float-pulling experience followed by time in a special viewing room at the Waqoo Naritasan Monzen hotel.

One night’s accommodation at Waqoo Naritasan Monzen with breakfast and dinner are also included in the deal, all for 84,000 yen.

These tours prove that the area around Narita Airport really is home to some great hidden gems. So if you’re passing through the region, or looking for something to do during a long layover, these Transit & Stay tours are a great way to explore outside the airport and experience a lesser-known side of Japan with the help of a local.

Reservations for the free tours open on 15 September and can be made here, while the paid tours are available to purchase now from this site.

title: Japan’s double-decker portable rice cooker/bento maker is better than ever with new version
description: Now there’s even more to be thankful to Thanko for. Japanese gadget maker Thanko has repeatedly shown its knack for innovations to be grateful for, but the company’s best idea of all is arguably its One-Person Rice Cooker Series. These compact kitchen appliances let you cook enough rice for a single serving, and their easy […]
content:
Now there’s even more to be thankful to Thanko for.

Japanese gadget maker Thanko has repeatedly shown its knack for innovations to be grateful for, but the company’s best idea of all is arguably its One-Person Rice Cooker Series. These compact kitchen appliances let you cook enough rice for a single serving, and their easy portability means that you can take them with you and cook your rice at your office desk or wherever else you need to be in the early part of the day, letting you enjoy freshly steamed rice once your lunch break comes around.

Of course, even Japanese people don’t eat just rice for lunch, so Thanko also makes two-tier one-person rice cookers. The bottom section is for cooking the rice, and the steam that rises from it is channeled into the upper section stacked on top of it, where it can cook, reheat, or thaw whatever vegetables, dumplings, curry roux, or other side dishes that you’re pairing with your rice.

With restaurant prices rising, Thanko says it’s seeing even higher demand than usual for its one-person rice cookers, and so the company’s designers have made a few improvements. First, they’ve managed to make the cooking process even speedier, and it now takes just 14 minutes to have a batch of rice ready to eat. They’ve added a timer function that will automatically start the cooking process one, two, or three hours after you set it. This new feature was added in order to make the one-person rice cooker easier to use with brown rice, which benefits from a longer soaking period than white rice, and thus increase the variety of meals that can be made with the device.

The one-person rice cooker is even a handy option for car camping, since it’ll work with vehicle power outlets as long as they put out at a voltage of at least 300 watts.

And yes, it’s still as compact as ever and easily breaks down into its component parts for easy cleaning.

▼ The parts shown at the bottom left are even dishwasher-safe.

The new and improved double-decker one-person rice cooker is priced at 8,980 yen (US$56) and just went on sale this week through the Thanko online store here.

title: Wait, some Shinkansen trains already have private booths that only cost 1,500 yen for an hour?
description: High-speed serenity has been low-key available on the Shinkansen for a long time with hardly anyone noticing it. A new Supreme Class is coming to Shinkansen trains this fall, offering luxurious private cabins for those with deep pockets. It turns out, though, that some bullet trains in Japan have quietly had available private booths for […]
content:
High-speed serenity has been low-key available on the Shinkansen for a long time with hardly anyone noticing it.

A new Supreme Class is coming to Shinkansen trains this fall, offering luxurious private cabins for those with deep pockets. It turns out, though, that some bullet trains in Japan have quietly had available private booths for years, and at very affordable prices.

If you’re wondering how this service has managed to escape the attention of so many travelers in Japan, it’s because the private booth is only offered on certain trains, and can only be reserved by certain passengers. Specifically, it’s only found on N700S-series Nozomi Shinkansen trains running on the Tokaido and Sanyo lines (i.e. between Tokyo and Fukuoka’s Hakata Station), and the booth can only be booked by passengers who’ve also purchased a regular seat in Car 7. The booth is located in the connecting area between Cars 7 and 8, and is equipped with two chairs, a counter, standard and USB power outlets, and a window so that you can watch the scenery zoom by from your private space.

You can use the booth either by yourself or with one other traveling companion, and rather than booking it for the length of your trip, it can be reserved, in 10-minute increments, for a block of time up to two hours.

So what’s the surcharge, on top of your Car 7 regular class Shinkansen ticket, to use this private booth? Hardly anything. Prices are just 200 yen (US$1.25) per 10 minutes up to a half-hour, and 300 yen per 10 minutes between 30 and 60 minutes, which works out to 600 yen for a 30-minute session or 1,500 yen for a full hour (payment is done by credit card). Things get a little pricier after that, with 90 minutes costing 2,500 yen and two hours 4,000 yen, but still, this a pretty affordable pocket of serene solitude.

Another likely reason this booth has largely escaped attention from travel fans is that, despite being available since 2022, it hasn’t been pitched to luxury travelers. In fact, JR calls it the Business Booth, and its exclusive availability to Car 7 on N700S Nozomi trains is because Car 7 is designated as the S Work car, which is promoted as being a car for passengers who need to get some work done during their ride. As such, the Business Booth isn’t outfitted with swanky interior fittings, and was primarily designed as a place where you can open up your laptop, lay out some documents, and make phone calls or hold video conferences with professional colleagues. All that said, it still remains a place you can have all to yourself for a while during your Shinkansen journey, even if all you want to do is relax.

Use of the Business Booth cannot be reserved ahead of time. Instead, after boarding you can check for/claim available time blocks via a QR code displayed at the booth’s entrance or on a pamphlet at your seat.

And, once again, the Business Booth is exclusive to N700S Nozomi trains, and if you’re looking for one, JR Central allows you to check which Shinkansen of that class are running on the current day by clicking on the button labeled ビジネスブースを搭載している今日の列車はこちら on their official website here.
